name: Kajaman
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The languages of Borneo: a comprehensive classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. (Kejaman primary data from Long Liten; sec. 2.3.1 Kajang pp. 92-98; Appendix 2 Melanau and Kajang wordlist p. 476ff.)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Nothing on where stress falls in Kejaman. Only relevant remark (p. 98): 'Note that Kajang languages regularly geminate consonants after schwa, which prevented *-əb- from weakening to *-əv-. In Kejaman, gemination surfaces as a glottal stop+consonant cluster rather than pure gemination.' Stress is described explicitly only for other Bornean groups (Merap, Segai-Modang, Hliboi).

sources.citation: Blust, Robert & Alexander D. Smith. 2014. A bibliography of the languages of Borneo (and Madagascar). Phillips, ME: Borneo Research Council.
sources.note: Bibliographic only: Strickland 1995 'Chapter 3, Language contains 13 pages of basic information on orthography and grammar'; Strickland 1988 SMJ 39(60):67-75; Aichner 1958; Bibi Aminah 2000 (sociolinguistic).

sources.citation: Strickland, S. S. 1995. Materials for the study of Kejaman-Sekapan oral tradition, Chapter 7: Notes to the sung narrative (pp. 389-502) and Chapter 9: Notes to the prose narrative (pp. 552-610). Sarawak Museum Journal XLIX(70), Special Monograph 8. (SMJ site hosts only 8-page excerpts of each; dois 10.61507/smj22-1995-4etx-07, -2xcs-09.)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: Harvard print copy (Scan & Deliver or loan): TOZ Offsite Storage MUS.17.4 (49:70)
sources.note: Lexical/philological notes to verses; no statement on word stress in the excerpts. Part I of the monograph (incl. Chapter 3 'Language', ~13 pp. of orthography/phonological notes and grammar per Blust & Smith 2014 and Kroeger 1998) is not hosted online.

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2023. Reconstructing non-contrastive stress in Austronesian and the role of the mora in stress shift, gemination and vowel shift. Diachronica.
sources.note: No Kejaman statement. For the sister language SEKAPAN [skp]: 'Smith (2017a) also recorded final stress where the penultimate syllable contains a schwa in Sekapan' (p. [14]) and 'In Sekapan, another Western Indonesian language of Borneo, final-syllable onsets automatically lengthen after a penultimate schwa, and stress is shifted to the final syllable (Smith 2017a)' with examples bəbaw [bəbːáw] 'tall', məjat [məjːát] 'to pull' (p. [26]); context implies otherwise-penultimate stress as in Mukah Melanau (Blust 1988:178) and Kayan.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian languages (revised ed.). Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: Mentions Kejaman only for its voiced labiovelar stop gw (p. 185); nothing on Kejaman stress.

sources.citation: Kroeger, Paul R. 1998. Language classification in Sarawak: a status report. Sarawak Museum Journal LIII(74): 137-173 (pre-publication draft).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 4.6 and 5.1b survey Kajang documentation: names 'the Kejaman phonological notes and text materials in Strickland (1995)' and 'Bibi Aminah Abdul Ghani. 1994 (ms). Kejaman wordlist and phonological sketch' as the only descriptive materials; Urquhart 1955 and Ray 1913 wordlists.
